title: The Monster's Snowman Problem
markdown:
Snowflakes, fat and silent, turned the Whispering Pines Inn into a white puffball high in the craggy mountains, warm as a dragon’s sneeze. Candles flickered, and the shadows they threw looked, if you were in the mood, like sprites practising a dance. The hearth crackled. The air smelled of pine needles, roasting chestnuts, and whatever the wind had decided to keep to itself. Down in the valley the museum would be locking its cases for the night. Up here, the inn had built its welcome in the middle of the floor.

The inn was not cozy for its current guests. A delegation of monsters, usually as loud as a goblin market on a feast day, sat hunched around a big oak table. Bright scales had gone dull. Magnificent horns drooped. Fearsome snarls had become weary rumbling sighs.

“Honestly, Willow,” whispered Fizzwick. His knobbly green ears vibrated. Fizzwick was the mayor’s chief clerk. He got flustered if a quill nib broke. “They look dreadful. As if they have all lost their favourite socks. What could upset such powerful beings?”

Willow, the mayor’s daughter, had more sense than a herd of wise old owls. Sturdy boots planted. Gaze sharp. She saw a tangled problem and began untangling it, knot by knot. “They arrived two hours ago, stomping like grumpy giants. Now they sulk. Distinguished company: Grolf, Zephyr, even old Grumblesnort.” Her eye landed on the spectacular, if over-the-top, festive display in the room’s centre.

Twinkling lights wove through pine. Crimson baubles gleamed. Most prominently stood a magnificent, impossibly fluffy white snowman, large sacks stuffed with soft down, a bright orange carrot for a nose, two smooth black pebbles for eyes. Cheerful winter hospitality, or so Master Bramble had intended.

“Perhaps,” Willow said, fingers tapping her chin, “it is the snowman. It is rather grand.”

Fizzwick gulped. “The snowman? Master Bramble said it was a symbol of good cheer.”

Master Bramble, whose belly seemed permanently at the edge of his apron, waddled over, wiping his hands. “Indeed. Finest goose-down stuffing. Cost a pretty penny. Took Lior and me a good half-day.” He beamed, oblivious to the weather at the monster table.

A hulking creature with fur like emerald moss and eyes like molten amber—the Stone-Troll Grolf, known for booming laughter—let out a low rumble. “Good cheer. Winter hospitality. You call that a welcome?”

A sleek winged creature whose scales shimmered like a rainbow after rain—the Sky-Serpent Zephyr—coiled its long tail. “It is deeply offensive. Profoundly disrespectful.”

Willow’s practical mind whirred. Offensive. A plump snowman. “Why?”

“Because,” Grolf rumbled, pointing a claw thick as a tree trunk, “that thing mocks our ancestors. White. Fluffy. Cold. Lifeless. Our greatest fear, our deepest sorrow, paraded as decoration.”

Fizzwick yelped and scrambled behind Willow’s legs. “Fear? Of a down-stuffed snowman?”

“Not just a snowman, you little squeaker,” Zephyr hissed, voice like a sharp wind. “A mockery of the Great White Silence. The eternal frost that claims all. The stillness that has swallowed so many of our kind. You put it on display like a trophy. As if you relish its cold embrace.”

The monsters grew agitated. To them the vast silent icy wilderness was a place of profound respect. Brave explorers and hardy hunters had been lost to its frozen embrace. The cheerful snowman looked like a caricature of solemn tradition: a grinning skull at a memorial. Tinsel looked like icy tendrils of doom. The bright red baubles, cheerful to humans, looked like bloodstains on ancestral snow.

The inn had meant fun. Therefore the monsters heard insult.

Master Bramble sputtered, face turning red. “It is just for fun. We never meant harm. Happy holidays.”

“Intention is a poor shield against a deep wound, Master Bramble,” said a quiet thoughtful voice from the stable doors.

Everyone turned. Lior the Bumbling, the inn’s stablehand, known for a gentle nature and a tendency to trip, stood with dreamy eyes gone sharp, a small weathered bucket in his hands. He shuffled forward with quiet purpose.

“I watch,” Lior said. “And I listen. You see your traditions in the snow, the quiet reverence. They see a happy picture for children. Both are true. But one voice was louder. It drowned out the other.” He looked at Willow. “The museum in the valley keeps ancient things in special cases. They shine like moonlit aquariums. They show respect by showing, not by making a loud cheerful spectacle of what is sacred.”

Willow’s eyes lit. A museum. Respect by showing. Therefore they did not need to destroy the snowman. They needed to transform the display. Show the beauty of the Silence, not only its cold.

The monsters looked sceptical. Transform. Into a sad snowman?

“We can add to it,” Willow said. “Majesty, not mockery. The quiet strength it takes to survive. Fizzwick, do you still have those dark blue ribbons from Master Bramble’s birthday presents?”

Fizzwick, trembling less, produced a roll of midnight-blue ribbon.

“And Lior, smooth grey stones from the riverbed, the kind a thousand years of water have finished. And gnarled branches from the old oak that has seen so many winters.”

Lior nodded. “I know just the ones.”

The inn buzzed with a new kind of hurry. Willow directed. Lior, with quiet knowledge of the wilderness and steadier hands than his nickname allowed, gathered materials. Fizzwick tied ribbons with surprising deftness. The monsters watched, gloom thinning, as the decorations were rearranged.

They moved the snowman slightly aside, giving him a contemplative part. Dark blue ribbons draped like a cloak of night sky. Smooth grey stones at his feet, silent markers. Weathered branches stood like sentinels against an imagined storm. The crimson baubles, no longer bloodstains, became distant stars peeking through frost.

The display still held cheer, but now it was woven with a solemn beauty: winter’s resilient power, and the stars that guide lost souls home. Not an insult. A tribute.

Grolf stepped forward, massive, amber eyes scanning every detail. He grunted, close to a sigh of relief. “This shows understanding. This acknowledges the respect we hold.”

Zephyr dipped an iridescent head. “The Silence is seen. Our sorrow is understood, not belittled.”

Master Bramble, bewildered but relieved, bowed. “I am truly sorry for our ignorance. We were blind to your traditions.”

Willow did not give a speech about perspectives. She looked at Lior, who gave a small almost imperceptible nod, and at Fizzwick, who had stopped hiding and was already winding leftover ribbon into a tidy coil, because unused ribbon made him nervous in a different way. The monsters’ voices regained their hearty tones. Grolf asked for chestnuts. Zephyr asked, politely, whether the lights might be dimmed a fraction. Master Bramble, still pink, dimmed them. Outside, the snow was a silent blanket. The snowman, in his new cloak, kept watch without grinning quite so hard, which was how you knew the inn had learned to lower its voice.
characters: Willow (practical mayor's child), Fizzwick (an anxious goblin clerk)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic story for confident middle-grade readers
